title: Impact of Guidance and Interaction Strategies for LLM Use on Learner Performance and Perception
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW2)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different guidance strategies shape learners’ interactions with large language models (LLMs), especially their performance, confidence, trust, and help-seeking behavior. The authors argue that the educational value of LLMs depends not just on whether learners use them, but on how they are guided to engage with them. They ask how pedagogically informed guidance strategies affect learner-LLM interaction patterns, task performance, confidence in using LLMs, trust in LLM responses, and self-confidence in problem solving.

The intervention consists of four guidance strategies for LLM use: a list of suggestions, example-based instruction, metacognitive questioning, and a "solve then refine with LLM" approach. These were examined in two empirical studies. Study 1 was a formative randomized factorial classroom study in an undergraduate computer science databases course (N=145 completing the assignment) at a North American university, where students used a GPT-3-based chatbot to support assignment work. Study 2 was a randomized online experiment on Prolific (N=356) in which adult participants solved elementary- and high-school-level math problems using either a prompted or unprompted GPT-3 chatbot and one of the guidance conditions or no instruction.

Across both studies, the paper does not examine writing instruction, motivation outcomes, or a high-school classroom ChatGPT writing-feedback trial. Instead, it focuses on undergraduate CS learning and adult crowdworkers solving math problems. In the classroom study, guidance changed the kinds of first queries students asked; structured guidance reduced unrelated queries and some forms reduced verbatim copying of assignment prompts. There were modest differences in homework scores across conditions, with the self-first "solve then refine" approach appearing less helpful for homework performance than some other guidance strategies, but the study is explicitly framed as formative and underpowered. In the Prolific experiment, neither guidance type nor prompted versus unprompted LLM produced statistically significant differences in task performance.

The main conclusions are that guidance meaningfully shapes interaction patterns and perceptions, but does not reliably improve objective performance in the controlled online study. Guidance briefly increased confidence in using LLMs, but this confidence fell after actual task use; trust in LLM responses also declined after experience. The paper emphasizes that teachers can shape more productive LLM-supported learning environments, but it does not provide evidence relevant to a secondary-school writing intervention, and it is not the alleged 2026 randomized trial with implausibly large motivation effects. Therefore, it should not be treated as the suspected high-school ChatGPT writing-feedback study for quantitative synthesis on that topic.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper includes a genuine randomized controlled experiment in Study 2 with n=356 and clearly described conditions, but it is not a high-school writing/ChatGPT feedback study and the main outcomes relevant here are confidence/trust and math performance, with several findings reported descriptively and limited effect-size reporting. It therefore has credible experimental design with some concerns rather than blue-tier causal evidence for the retrieved topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not show clear academic gains from the LLM intervention; math performance differences were null, while confidence/trust effects were mixed and in some cases negative after use. For the retrieved synthesis question, impact is unclear and not supportive of a positive educational effect.

interventions.use_case: GPT-3/LLM chatbot used as a teaching assistant/tutor for undergraduate database assignments and for adults solving elementary and high-school-level math problems, comparing guidance strategies for how learners interact with the chatbot.

Structured software-delivered instructional guidance conditions (list-based suggestions, example-based instruction, metacognitive questioning, solve-then-refine workflow) layered around chatbot use to shape learner interaction patterns.

finding.finding_summary: In the Prolific randomized controlled experiment (n=356), learner+AI performance on four math problems did not differ significantly across five guidance strategies (Kruskal-Wallis chi-square(4)=0.13, p=1.00) or between prompted versus unprompted LLM conditions (Mann-Whitney W=15025, p=0.37). Exploratory subgroup means suggested some variation (e.g., example-based guidance with unprompted LLM 68.13%±2.68% vs prompted 58.09%±4.32%), but these were not reported as statistically reliable treatment effects.
finding.measure: Accuracy/average score on 4 multiple-choice math problems

finding.finding_summary: In the formative undergraduate database classroom study (n=145), homework scores showed small descriptive differences across guidance conditions, with solve-then-refine guidance appearing somewhat less favorable than other guidance types for assignment performance. However, no inferential test establishing a statistically reliable effect on database learning performance is reported in the excerpt, and exam performance remained broadly similar across conditions.
finding.measure: Homework score and exam score in undergraduate database course

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies confidence, trust, and self-perception rather than motivation. In the Prolific RCT (n=356), confidence in ability to use LLMs changed significantly over time (Friedman chi-square(2)=72.82, p<0.001): it increased after guidance (Mean 4.51, SD 1.49 to Mean 5.19, SD 1.66) but dropped after task completion (Mean 4.57, SD 1.81). Trust in LLM responses also declined significantly after actual use (initial Mean 4.36, SD 1.36; final Mean 3.49, SD 1.80; Friedman chi-square(2)=80.31, p<0.001), while confidence in one's math-solving ability showed no significant pre-post change (p=0.079).
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in using LLMs, trust in LLM responses, self-confidence in solving math; Likert-scale surveys across multiple stages
finding.std_deviation: Reported for key measures: initial LLM-use confidence SD=1.49, post-guidance SD=1.66, post-task SD=1.81; initial trust SD=1.36, final trust SD=1.80; math self-confidence pre SD=1.41, post SD=1.62

finding.finding_summary: Structured guidance altered learner interaction patterns with the chatbot in the classroom study (138 of 145 students used the LLM), reducing unrelated queries for list-based suggestions, metacognitive questioning, and solve-then-refine conditions, while example-based instruction unexpectedly increased unrelated/test queries. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that guidance shapes metacognitive engagement and help-seeking behavior, but they do not report standardized effect sizes for these differences.
finding.measure: Categorized first-query behavior to the LLM (verbatim copying, rewording, unrelated testing, conceptual clarification)
finding.study_size: n=138 LLM users within n=145 classroom sample
